reverse_outline.summary: Three-point preview: checkout creates the order once, later messages need separate states and keys, the order ends in documents with single writers and monthly matching
Opening failure: a paid order still shows unpaid, confusing warehouse and support
Part's scope: checkout asks owners for answers, then late, unordered or duplicate messages report payment, dispatch and delivery
The rules the part sets, one per owner: single creation, keyed messages and one writer, separate states, ledger from documents matched to the bank
Running example: Eva's €235 order and its timeline from pending to monthly bank match
Each chapter opens on a past failure of a company without a shared order record
Checkout chapter: coordinating dependencies and creating one order, not tied to the thank-you page
Payments chapter: payment lifecycle, with duplicate refunds showing need for one writer and a shared retry identifier
Order management chapter: shared order home with separate payment, shipment and return states / when to adopt an OMS
Tax and ledger chapter: linking orders, invoices, payouts and bank / issuer of an e-invoice must track its delivery or rejection
Synthesis: provider message marks payment, look for the missing rule when systems disagree, start with checkout

Synthesis of the rules against the opening case.
The scene itself names the three who need the fact: the warehouse cannot tell whether to dispatch, support cannot answer.
PSP and webhook glossed; the closing sentence says what the messages imply: 'may arrive late, out of order or twice'.
KEY POINTS callout states the argument in three lines; the body's p02 and p03 explain each bullet (except the invoice-sequence clause, recorded under known_before_new).
Figure 1's caption says what it shows (one creation, one hub, ledger fed by documents, scheduled reconciliation) and p03 just before it states the same rules.

Figure 2's caption says what it shows: checkout creates it, the provider settles it, the order record holds it, the ledger ends it. Its placement is a flow point, recorded under flow_is_followable.
Says what the failures are for: each chapter opens on one.

'explain why a refund needs one authorized writer and an identifier shared across retries'.
The fleece case is followed by 'The chapter shows how to represent partial completion honestly'.

sequence: 'sets that money status beside the others' picks up the payments chapter's money status.

results.quote: One order passes through four owners in Part III: checkout creates it, the payment provider settles it, the order record holds it, and the ledger ends it.
results.finding: Both flow readers lost the thread at Figure 2: it sits after Eva's paragraph but illustrates the four owners of the rules paragraph, so it reads as repeating Figure 1 away from its text (flowA) or as being about Eva's timeline (flowB); both suggest moving it beside Figure 1. The spec places it as evidence of Eva's order and rejected moving it in round 2; either the caption ties it to Eva's order (draft) or the figure moves (spec), so the author decides.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 1 (Figure 2 sits after the Eva paragraph but illustrates the four owners named in the rules paragraph)

results.quote: The company still has no shared order record, and each chapter opens on one of its failures from the months before Eva's order.
results.finding: Both readers re-read 'still has no shared order record' right after Eva's order 'goes right': 'still' as of when, and how did her order go right without one? The prose leaves the time and the contrast unresolved (flowB suggests 'before Eva's order').
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 2 ('still' as of when? ... how her order went right without one)

results.quote: Not every Kestrel & Pine order went well.
results.finding: Both readers felt the return from Eva's successful order back to failures as a step backwards (flowA) or a restart that repeats the opening scene (flowB). This comes from the declared order (failure, rules, Eva's order, failures, chapters), which the spec's rationale defends; flowA proposes moving the failures line next to the opening incident. The order itself is the cause, so the author decides.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 3 ('Not every Kestrel & Pine order went well' repeats what the opening scene already showed, so it felt briefly like a restart)

results.quote: So the part sets rules, one chapter for each of the order's four owners: checkout, the payment provider, the order record and finance's ledger.
results.finding: Both readers paused at calling checkout (flowA: the callout says checkout owns 'none of the facts it writes') and the external payment provider (flowB) 'owners' of the order. The word clashes with the callout and with Part I's sense of an owner as the system of record for a fact; a different word (e.g. 'stations' or 'stages', as Figure 2's relay) would remove it.
results.corroborated_by: flowB, item 5 (calling an external provider an owner of the order made me pause)

results.quote: initially with payment pending, like the opening's order.
results.finding: flowA had to work out whether 'the opening' meant this page's first paragraph or the book's opening. One reader only.

results.quote: Once the order's shipments are recorded, [[tax-invoicing-and-ledger]] connects
results.finding: flowA found the bridge from shipments to a money-and-documents chapter off, because the page has not said that invoices are issued per shipment. One reader only.

results.quote: One writer per money movement, one invoice sequence per legal entity
results.finding: flowA: the callout's 'one invoice sequence per legal entity' never comes back in the body. One flow reader only (also recorded under known_before_new).

results.quote: (a payout is its transfer of collected money to the merchant)
results.finding: flowA: the parenthetical gloss slows an already long sentence. One reader only.

results.quote: the provider's message, not the thank-you page, marks it paid
results.finding: flowB: the opening scene never mentions the thank-you page, so the closing's payoff 'only half lands'; the thank-you page first appears in the checkout chapter entry. One reader only.
'authorization, collection, settlement and payout' are named as the payments chapter's subject, as the spec allows ('only named here'); payout is glossed in p03.
'every message carries a key, so a repeat changes nothing' states what the key does; idempotency is known from Part I.
Peppol is glossed: 'the network for structured invoices'; PSP, webhook, payout and OMS are glossed too.
'closes April's books in May': the terms reader judged it minor and guessable from context.

results.quote: The ledger is posted from documents
results.finding: 'Posted' is accounting jargon (writing an entry into the ledger) and 'finance's ledger' is only a thin gloss of the ledger; the audience is new to commerce architecture and the ledger's posting rules are on does_not_know. Reported by the terms reader; no flow reader reported it.

results.quote: One writer per money movement, one invoice sequence per legal entity
results.finding: Neither 'invoice sequence' (the unbroken, legally required numbering) nor 'legal entity' is explained, and the body never returns to it. Reported by the terms reader in this and earlier rounds; the spec's decision log keeps the callout as the author's wording, so a fix needs the author.
results.corroborated_by: flowA, item 6 (the key point 'one invoice sequence per legal entity' never comes back in the body)

results.finding: Opens on a puzzling scenario (a paid order that reads unpaid), as the spec's hook declares; no placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.
Does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new subtopic or evidence; it answers the opening and gives a course of action.

'Together, the chapters explain the opening's unpaid order: the provider's message, not the thank-you page, marks it paid' is stated by no chapter paragraph; 'When systems disagree, look first for the missing rule' is the so-what.
Returns to p01's paid order that reads unpaid and says what marks it paid. (flowB notes the thank-you page was not in the opening scene; recorded as a minor flow point.)

The cold reader of the introduction named the four chapters in order (checkout creating the order once despite retries; payment provider with keys and one writer per money action; the order record with separate states for money, parcels and returns; the ledger posted from documents with a monthly match of orders, payouts and the bank), the evidence (Kestrel & Pine failures, Eva's order, diagrams) and the tone. The payment stages are not in the introduction units, so their absence is expected.

The reader explained the webhook (server-to-server, may arrive late or twice) and that only the provider's message marks the order paid, and said the order needs separate states for money, shipments and returns in the order record and a key on every message so a repeat changes nothing. Matches expected.

The reader sent (a) to commerce-payments (one authorized writer, shared identifier, 212 refunds) and (b) to order-management (separate shipment states, partial completion, fleece before socks). Matches expected.
